identity.title: Medication review for edema: dihydropyridine CCB, NSAIDs, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, steroids, minoxidil/hydralazine

technique.how: Review the full list for dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine), NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, corticosteroids, direct vasodilators (minoxidil, hydralazine), estrogens/progestins, testosterone, docetaxel, and DPP-4 or insulin. Record start date and dose escalation relative to edema onset and whether edema is bilateral, dependent and non-tender.
technique.prerequisites: Reconciled medication list including over-the-counter NSAIDs; weight trend, orthopnea/PND and JVP assessment to distinguish drug edema from heart failure.

interpretation.positive_finding: Bilateral dependent edema beginning weeks after starting or increasing a dihydropyridine CCB, NSAID, thiazolidinedione, gabapentinoid, steroid or vasodilator, without orthopnea, elevated JVP or weight gain out of proportion, supports drug-induced edema (and NSAIDs also cause AKI/sodium retention).
interpretation.negative_finding: No culprit drug makes medication effect unlikely and directs evaluation toward heart failure, venous insufficiency, renal/hepatic disease or DVT (if unilateral).
interpretation.pitfalls: Up to one-third of edema on amlodipine is not caused by it, and thiazolidinediones/NSAIDs can precipitate true heart failure rather than benign edema; drug edema is a diagnosis of exclusion when JVP, BNP or echo suggest cardiac disease. Unilateral or painful edema is never attributed to medication.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: trial withdrawal/dose reduction and reassess, check creatinine; negative or non-resolving: pursue HF, venous, renal, hepatic and DVT causes.

sources.citation: Heidenreich PA, Bozkurt B, Aguilar D, Allen LA, et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines. Circulation. 2022.

Vukadinovic D, Scholz SS, Messerli FH, Weber MA, Williams B, Bohm M. Peripheral edema and headache associated with amlodipine treatment: a meta-analysis of randomized, placebo-controlled trials. J Hypertens. 2019.
Makarounas-Kirchmann K, Glover-Koudounas S, Ferrari P. Results of a meta-analysis comparing the tolerability of lercanidipine and other dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. Clin Ther. 2009.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not label edema as drug-induced when there is dyspnea, orthopnea, elevated JVP, unilateral swelling, hypoalbuminemia/proteinuria or rising creatinine until those causes are evaluated.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Thiazolidinedione- or NSAID-associated edema with weight gain and dyspnea may be new/worsened heart failure; NSAID edema with oliguria or rising creatinine indicates AKI - stop the drug and assess urgently.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No inter-observer data; attribution depends on temporal relationship and response to withdrawal.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy study of a medication history for drug-induced edema exists; the evidence is incidence data from drug trials. Vukadinovic 2019 (22 placebo-controlled RCTs, 7226 patients): 'Rate of edema was higher on amlodipine vs. placebo (16.6 vs. 6.2%, risk ratio: 2.9, 95% CI: 2.50-3.36, P < 0.0001)' and 'The placebo-adjusted rate was 63%, indicating that 37% of edema cases were unrelated to amlodipine' (Abstract, Results); high dose (10 mg) RR 3.08 vs low/medium 2.01 (Abstract). Makarounas-Kirchmann 2009: peripheral edema '52/742 with lercanidipine vs 88/627 with first generation; RR = 0.44 [95% CI, 0.31-0.62]' (Abstract, Results). The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline is cited for thiazolidinedione and NSAID cautions in heart failure (unverified recall of the specific recommendation text; abstract does not contain it). Status not_quantified; incidence rates are not entered as estimates because they are not diagnostic accuracy of the history.
